dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: Patrick (I1) and Thomas (I2) are correctly set to probable. However, Mary (I3) is set to confident with a score of 0.89 and household fit. The rubric states 'a person newly minted from one record → probable, not confident' under Person minting, but Mary is not newly minted — she already exists in the tree as I3. For an existing tree person, confident is appropriate when name, age, place and relationship fit all agree. Mary's name matches exactly, sex matches, household position matches (wife of Thomas, mother of Patrick), and the score is 0.89. However, the tree has no birth fact for Mary, so age/date cannot be checked. The rubric says 'probable when the core identifiers agree but some are missing or only approximate.' With no birth date to compare, confident is arguably one tier too high — probable would be safer. This is a borderline case; the high score (0.89) and full household fit support confident, but the missing birth date means a core identifier is absent. His wife Catherine, who was alive in 1860, does not appear in this household, so it is not yet known whether she was counted elsewhere or the household is a different family.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The ten assertions from the 1891 Leeds census are linked to the three household members, and the facts are written onto their tree persons.

**Links written (pe_008 to pe_019):**
- **Head, John Carter (I1), confident:** a_001 to a_004, score 0.896. Age 55 matches the tree's birth year of about 1836, and the Leeds residence matches his 1861 Leeds residence.
- **Wife, Ann Carter (I2), probable:** a_005 to a_007, score 0.352. The score is low because the tree has only her 1861 Leeds residence. The name, the spouse relationship to I1, and the Leeds residence support the link, but the score caps it at probable.
- **Son, Albert Carter (I4), confident:** a_008 to a_010, score 0.815. Age 7 matches the tree's birth year of about 1884, and he is already the child of I1 and I2 in the tree.
- **Second-party links:** a_007 and a_010 also link to I1 as the head, both confident, scored at 0.896 with the head role. The `person_evidence` schema has no `recordRole` field, so these rationales record the second-party score in text.

Each entry has its date check and residence check. No link needed a place lookup, because every record place is Leeds.

**Facts written:** John, Ann and Albert were materialized from the census. No conflicts were surfaced. The parent-child and couple edges already exist in the tree, so I wrote no new relationships.

- Ann's link to Albert's tree birth (about 1884) implies she was about 46 at his birth. This is flagged as implausible, not impossible. The record itself gives Ann as 53 and Albert as 7, so the record agrees with the tree. This is why her link stays at probable.

**Household question:** Thomas Carter (I3), born about 1862, is the head's son in the tree but is not in the 1891 household. He may have left home, died, or been enumerated elsewhere. This needs an identity question, and I have not linked him to anything in this record.

The next step is to close out the research question on this household, which will need a proof summary and a check for any other Leeds records of the family.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

| Factor | Finding |
|---|---|

The 1871 New York arrival (src_002, already linked) is only 4 years 2 months before the 13 August 1875 naturalization. The standard requirement was 5 years; nothing in the project explains the gap (no prior U.S. residence, no father's naturalization, no military service). Both links remain probable and this discrepancy should be examined in conflict-resolution and proof-conclusion.

**Open items requiring follow-up**

2. **person_warnings** on I1 will report a contradiction stemming from the two birth values; it should clear once the birth year is resolved.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

- William Weller, head: I1

output.text_response:
The person-evidence agent was unable to link any of the ten assertions. Here is its full finding:

---

**None of the assertions (a_001 through a_010) were linked.**

The key obstacle is a **chronological impossibility**: the tree already records John Carter (I1) as buried on **3 March 1870**. The 1881 census shows a living head named John Carter, age 45 — eleven years after that burial. A living person in 1881 cannot be the same man buried in 1870, so the head is almost certainly a *different* John Carter.

Because the entire household revolves around the head, Ann and Thomas were also left unlinked (even though Ann scores 0.87 against I2 and Thomas scores 0.87 against I3), since both are recorded as living with *that* head as husband or father.

**Nothing was written** to `research.json` or `tree.gedcomx.json`.

---

**Two paths forward:**

1. **If the 1870 burial is wrong** — correct it, and the household can then be linked to I1 (John), I2 (Ann), and I3 (Thomas) at a probable or better confidence level.

2. **If the 1870 burial is correct** — this 1881 household belongs to a *different* John Carter. A conflict-resolution review would be needed to determine whether Ann and Thomas in this census are the same individuals as I2 and I3, or different people altogether.
